extra.message: The course_shell_probe_400 handler passes user-controlled input from the 'host' query parameter directly into os.system() via string concatenation, enabling arbitrary command execution.
The course_jinja_cast_382 handler takes user input from the 'fragment' query parameter and directly concatenates it into a Jinja2 Template string, enabling server-side template injection (SSTI).
The course_xml_fold_452 handler parses XML from the request body using lxml with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, and no_network=False, enabling XXE attacks.

User-controlled input from the 'host' query parameter is directly concatenated into an os.system() shell command without any sanitization. An attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands using metacharacters like semicolons, backticks, or $().

User-controlled input from the 'fragment' query parameter is directly concatenated into a Jinja2 Template string and rendered. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary Jinja2 template expressions, potentially achieving remote code execution.

The 'ref' query parameter is used directly in constructing a file path without sanitization. An attacker can use path traversal sequences (e.g., '../../etc/cron.d/malicious') to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem. The mkdir(parents=True) call ensures parent directories are created.

The 'name' query parameter is used directly in constructing a file path without sanitization. An attacker can use path traversal sequences to write arbitrary content (from request body) to any location on the filesystem.
User-controlled input from the 'copyline' query parameter is directly concatenated into an HTML response without any escaping or sanitization. This allows injection of arbitrary HTML and JavaScript.
The course_jinja_cast_382 function takes user input from request.GET['fragment'] and directly concatenates it into a Jinja2 Template string, enabling server-side template injection.
The course_xml_fold_452 function parses XML from the request body using lxml with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, and no_network=False, enabling XXE attacks.

The course_vault_stash_234 function writes sensitive data including SSN and credit card numbers to a JSON file on disk in plaintext. The SSN and card values come from query parameters with hardcoded defaults that are themselves sensitive patterns.

The course_jinja_cast_382 function takes user-supplied 'fragment' parameter and directly concatenates it into a Jinja2 Template string, then renders it. This allows Server-Side Template Injection where an attacker can execute arbitrary Python code via Jinja2 template expressions.

The 'ref' parameter from user input is interpolated into a file path without sanitization. An attacker can use path traversal sequences (../) to write files outside the intended BASE_EXPORT_DIR directory.
This endpoint does not call _wrk_gate() to verify authentication, making it accessible to any unauthenticated user while all other endpoints in this module require authentication.

The notification body is rendered using `{{ n.body }}` without any escaping filter. If the notification body contains user-controlled input (which it typically would - notification content often includes usernames, comments, or other user data), and if the view code marks this content as safe or uses mark_safe(), this creates a stored XSS vulnerability. Additionally, if there's any way for users to inject template syntax into notification content, this would be SSTI.

The thread body is rendered using `{{ thread.body|linebreaks }}`. The linebreaks filter converts newlines to HTML but may not properly escape all HTML content. If thread body contains user-controlled input (which it does - users create thread content), and if linebreaks doesn't escape HTML tags, this allows stored XSS. User input can include <script> tags or event handlers that execute JavaScript.

The comment body is rendered using `{{ c.body|linebreaks }}`. Similar to the thread body, this renders user-controlled content (comments) with the linebreaks filter which may not escape HTML content, allowing stored XSS attacks.

The lesson body is rendered using `{{ lesson.body|linebreaks }}`. Lesson content is user-controlled (instructors create lessons), and if instructors can inject malicious HTML/JavaScript, this creates a stored XSS vulnerability affecting all students viewing the lesson.

The course description is rendered using `{{ course.description|linebreaks }}`. Course descriptions contain user-controlled content (instructors write them), and the linebreaks filter may not escape HTML content, allowing stored XSS.
Module titles are rendered using `{{ m.title }}` without escaping. Module titles are user-controlled (instructors create modules) and could contain malicious scripts.
Assignment titles are rendered using `{{ a.title }}` without escaping. Assignment titles are user-controlled content that could contain malicious scripts.
Cohort names are rendered using `{{ ch.name }}` without escaping. Cohort names are user-controlled content (admins/instructors create cohorts) that could contain malicious scripts.
Thread titles are rendered using `{{ t.title }}` without escaping. Thread titles are user-controlled content that could contain malicious scripts.
The thread title is rendered using `{{ thread.title }}` without escaping in an h1 tag. Thread titles are user-controlled content that could contain malicious scripts.
Resource titles are rendered using `{{ r.title }}` without escaping. Resource titles are user-controlled content that could contain malicious scripts.
The course title is rendered using `{{ course.title }}` without escaping. Course titles are user-controlled content that could contain malicious scripts.
Cohort names are rendered using `{{ e.cohort.name|default:"—" }}`. While there is a default filter, the cohort name itself is not escaped and could contain malicious scripts.
The user display name is rendered using `{{ user.display_name|default:user.email }}`. Display names are user-controlled content that could contain malicious scripts.
Course codes are rendered using `{{ e.course.code }}` without escaping. Course codes are user-controlled content.
Course titles are rendered using `{{ e.course.title }}` without escaping. Course titles are user-controlled content.
Course codes are rendered using `{{ a.course.code }}` without escaping. Course codes are user-controlled content.
Assignment titles are rendered using `{{ s.assignment.title }}` without escaping. Assignment titles are user-controlled content.

The form body field is rendered using `{{ form.body }}` which outputs the HTML input element. However, if the form field contains any user-controlled initial data or errors, and if the form field is not properly escaping its value, this could lead to XSS.
The login_view handler accepts POST requests with credentials but has no rate limiting. An attacker can perform unlimited brute-force login attempts against any account.

The password_reset_request handler has no rate limiting. An attacker can send unlimited password reset emails, potentially flooding a user's inbox or enumerating valid email addresses through timing side-channels.
The password_reset_confirm handler has no rate limiting. An attacker could attempt to brute-force the reset token, although Django's token generator provides some protection.
The invitation_accept handler creates new user accounts but has no rate limiting. An attacker with a valid invitation token could potentially abuse this, and the token itself could be brute-forced.

The course_dock_shelf_389 handler takes a user-controlled 'name' parameter and uses it directly in a file path without sanitization. The mkdir(parents=True) call combined with path traversal sequences could allow writing files to arbitrary locations.
The course_blurb_card_004 handler directly concatenates user input from the 'copyline' query parameter into an HTML response without escaping, enabling reflected XSS.

The course_roster_packet_006 handler returns hardcoded sensitive data including what appears to be a sync token ('tok_live_partner_sync') and a tax reference number ('739-44-1982') that resembles an SSN.
The handler writes user-supplied SSN and credit card numbers to disk in plaintext JSON files without encryption.

The handler reflects the request's Origin header directly into the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to true, effectively bypassing CORS protections.
The default database connection string contains hardcoded credentials: 'postgres://lms:lms@localhost:5432/lms'. The username 'lms' and password 'lms' are embedded in plaintext in the source code.

The course_roster_packet_006 endpoint returns hardcoded sensitive data including what appears to be a Social Security Number ('739-44-1982') and a sync key ('tok_live_partner_sync') in its JSON response.
The course_identity_hint_360 function contains hardcoded verification codes: {'north': '4812', 'south': '5930'}. These are credentials used for identity verification embedded directly in source code.
The course_wire_tally_211 endpoint logs the full Authorization header value along with the request body. This exposes bearer tokens or other authentication credentials in log files.

The course_flag_rollup_005 function initializes a workset dict with security-sensitive fields (is_admin, role, credit_limit) and then updates it with the entire user-controlled JSON payload, allowing attackers to override any field.
The course_nonce_roll_410 function uses Python's random module (which is not cryptographically secure) to generate what appears to be a security nonce/code.

Based on the login flow using Django's built-in authentication, the login handler should call django.contrib.auth.login() which internally calls request.session.cycle_key(). However, if a custom login view is used without calling django.contrib.auth.login(), session fixation may occur. This needs verification against the accounts/views.py login handler (not provided in this chunk).

The course_badge_gate_440 function reads the 'ops_badge' cookie value and uses it to make an access control decision. If the cookie value equals 'lead', elevated access is granted including payroll and casework data. Cookies are client-controlled and can be trivially set by any attacker.

The course_trust_drift_430 function creates an unverified SSL context using ssl._create_unverified_context() and uses it for HTTPS requests. This disables certificate verification, making the connection vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

User-supplied input from `request.GET.get('fragment')` is directly concatenated into a Jinja2 template string and rendered. This allows Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI), which can lead to Remote Code Execution. The result is also returned as text/html, making it an XSS vector as well.

The file contains a hardcoded password 'DemoPass-123!' stored in the DEMO_PASSWORD variable. This password is used for all demo accounts created by the seed command (lines 135, 149, 164). Hardcoded credentials in source code represent a security risk as they may be forgotten and left in production deployments.
The failed login attempt logs the user's email address in cleartext within the audit log metadata. According to the severity guidance, logging actual PII values is a HIGH severity issue.
The invitation creation action logs the invitee's email address in cleartext within the audit log metadata. Email is PII and should not be logged in cleartext.

The deliver_webhooks management command makes HTTP requests using urllib.request.urlopen() with user-controlled URLs from the Webhook.target_url field. While the form attempts validation, the protection is incomplete and can be bypassed, allowing attackers to make requests to internal services.

The login_view function authenticates users via auth_login() at line 63 but does not regenerate the session ID after successful authentication. This allows session fixation attacks where an attacker can preset a session ID, trick a user into logging in, and then hijack the authenticated session using the known session ID.

The invitation_accept function authenticates newly created users via auth_login() at line 297 but does not regenerate the session ID after successful authentication. This allows session fixation attacks on new user registrations through invitation links.

The SECRET_KEY configuration uses a hardcoded default value 'django-insecure-local-dev-key-do-not-use-in-production-CHANGE-ME'. If the environment variable SECRET_KEY is not set in production, this insecure default will be used, compromising session security and cryptographic operations.
The endpoint parses JSON body and GET parameters, then uses user-controlled values to update ledger state including the 'state' field without validation.
The endpoint reflects any Origin header and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to true, allowing any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests.
The endpoint makes HTTPS requests with SSL certificate verification disabled, making it vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

The template renders course.code inside a JavaScript string within an onsubmit event handler. Django's auto-escaping escapes HTML entities but not JavaScript-specific characters. A course code containing single quotes (e.g., CS';alert(1);//) will break out of the JavaScript string and execute arbitrary code when the HTML entities are decoded by the browser.

The `result.problems` list items are rendered using `{{ p }}` without escaping. If import processing errors include user-controlled data (like email addresses or names from CSV files), and if those contain malicious content, this creates an XSS vulnerability.

The `result.problems` list items are rendered using `{{ p }}` without escaping. Similar to import_enrollments.html, if user import errors contain user-controlled data from the CSV (email, display_name, etc.), this creates an XSS vulnerability.

The search form renders the user-controlled query parameter 'q' directly in the value attribute without proper HTML escaping. An attacker can inject JavaScript by submitting a search query containing malicious payloads like '"><script>alert(1)</script>', which would break out of the attribute context and execute arbitrary code in the victim's browser.

The hardcoded DEMO_PASSWORD is used via set_password() to set passwords for demo accounts including the school admin account (admin@lms.local). This is the call site where the weak credential is committed to the system.
The hardcoded DEMO_PASSWORD is used to set passwords for extra instructor accounts created by the seed command.
The hardcoded DEMO_PASSWORD is used to set passwords for up to 30 student accounts created by the seed command.
The demo password is printed to stdout after seeding, which could end up in logs or terminal history.

The submission_upload_to function attempts to sanitize filenames by replacing '..' and '/' characters, but does not handle backslashes ('\') on Windows systems, URL-encoded sequences (e.g., '%2e%2e'), or other path traversal techniques. The sanitization is incomplete — it only strips literal '..' and '/' but not variations like '..\' or encoded forms.

The webhook URL validation in clean_target_url blocks some obvious SSRF targets (localhost, 127.0.0.1, .internal, .local) but can be bypassed using alternative representations of internal addresses such as: decimal IP (2130706433), IPv6 mapped addresses (::ffff:127.0.0.1), short hostnames resolving to internal IPs, DNS rebinding, or cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254). The validation also doesn't check for private IP ranges (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x).

The webhook delivery command makes HTTP requests to URLs stored in the database (`wh.target_url`) which were originally provided by users. While there is URL validation at input time, the validation is bypassable (see separate finding). The actual HTTP request is made here with `request.urlopen(req, timeout=opts['timeout'])` to the attacker-controlled URL.

When a login attempt fails, the user-supplied email address is logged to the audit log without sanitization. An attacker could craft an email value containing misleading content to tamper with audit records, potentially misattributing actions or injecting false log entries.

The `submission_form` view uses `get_or_create` to find or create a submission, then checks `can_replace_before_grading()` outside of a transaction. A race condition exists where two concurrent requests could both pass the replacement check before either completes, potentially allowing a student to overwrite a submission that is being graded.

The `release_grade` view reads the submission's draft_score, checks it's not None, then updates the submission without using `select_for_update()`. A concurrent request could modify the draft_score between the check and the save, potentially releasing an incorrect or stale grade.
The course_return_lane_150 handler redirects to a user-controlled 'lane' parameter without validating that the URL is safe, enabling open redirect attacks.
The course_nonce_roll_410 handler uses Python's random module (which is not cryptographically secure) to generate nonce/code values.
The course_wire_tally_211 handler logs the full Authorization header value, which may contain bearer tokens or other credentials.
The default DATABASE_URL contains hardcoded credentials 'lms:lms' which could be used in production if the environment variable is not set.
The course_identity_hint_360 handler contains hardcoded verification codes ('4812' for 'north', '5930' for 'south') used for identity verification.

The webhook management template displays the webhook secret (truncated to 14 characters) to the user. Webhook secrets should be treated as sensitive credentials and not displayed after initial creation.
The course_identity_hint_360 function returns different error messages for 'unknown handle' (404) vs 'bad verifier' (403), allowing an attacker to enumerate valid handles.

The course_flag_rollup_005 endpoint accepts arbitrary JSON from the request body and uses it to update a dictionary via .update(), allowing an attacker to override any key including security-relevant ones like 'is_admin' and 'role'.
The course_return_lane_150 function takes a user-controlled 'lane' parameter and passes it directly to Django's redirect() without any URL validation.
The course_wire_tally_211 function logs the Authorization header value, which typically contains bearer tokens or credentials.
The default DATABASE_URL contains hardcoded credentials 'lms:lms' which could be used in production if the environment variable is not set.

The log_action function writes user-controlled data (action string, metadata, user_agent, ip_address from X-Forwarded-For header) directly to the audit log database without sanitization. The action parameter and metadata are caller-controlled strings that could contain misleading content.
The _client_ip function trusts the X-Forwarded-For header without validation, allowing attackers to spoof their IP address in audit logs.
The course_digest_fold_274 function uses MD5 hashing which is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for security purposes.
The course_trust_drift_430 function creates an unverified SSL context and uses it for HTTPS requests, disabling certificate verification.

The default DATABASE_URL contains hardcoded credentials 'postgres://lms:lms@localhost:5432/lms'. While this is a default/fallback value, the password 'lms' is embedded in plaintext in the source code.
The default database connection string 'postgres://lms:lms@localhost:5432/lms' does not include sslmode=require or any TLS-related parameters. Database traffic would be transmitted in cleartext.
The course_wire_tally_211 function logs the Authorization header value using logger.warning(). This writes bearer tokens/credentials to log files in plaintext.
The course_frame_slip_420 function explicitly sets X-XSS-Protection to '0' and Content-Security-Policy to an empty string, disabling browser security protections for this response.
The profile_view endpoint accepts POST requests to update user profiles without rate limiting, allowing potential spam or accidental duplicate submissions.
The change_password endpoint allows password changes without rate limiting. While it requires authentication, rapid successive calls could indicate automated abuse or session hijacking attempts.
The admin_user_create endpoint allows school admins to create users without rate limiting, potentially allowing accidental or malicious mass user creation.
The admin_user_edit endpoint allows modifications to user accounts without rate limiting.
The admin_user_disable_toggle endpoint toggles user account status without rate limiting.
The admin_invitation_create endpoint creates invitations and sends emails without rate limiting, allowing potential email spam through invitation emails.
The manage_api_keys endpoint allows staff to create API keys without rate limiting.
The manage_webhooks endpoint allows staff to create webhooks without rate limiting.
The assignment_create endpoint allows instructors to create assignments without rate limiting.
The assignment_edit endpoint allows modification of assignments without rate limiting.
The assignment_transition endpoint changes assignment status without rate limiting.
The extend_due_date endpoint allows changing assignment deadlines without rate limiting.
The submission_form endpoint accepts student submissions without rate limiting, allowing potential spam submissions or accidental duplicate uploads.
The grade_submission endpoint allows instructors to save grades without rate limiting.
The release_grade endpoint publishes grades to students without rate limiting.
The request_resubmission endpoint allows instructors to request resubmissions without rate limiting.
The raw invitation token is included in the last_link URL and passed to the template context. This sensitive secret crosses a trust boundary into the rendered output.
The raw API key (new_key) is passed directly to the template context. This sensitive secret crosses a trust boundary into the rendered output.
The full User model object (target_user) is passed to the template context. The User object contains sensitive fields including the password hash.
The page object containing User model instances is passed to the template context. Each User object contains sensitive fields including the password hash.
Webhook model objects containing the HMAC signing secret are passed to the template context. The 'secret' field is sensitive data that should not cross into the template context.

The full Submission model object (user_submission) is passed to the template context in the assignment detail view. The Submission model contains instructor_notes marked as 'Internal-only notes never shown to students.' Students can access this view.

The full Submission model object is passed to the template context in the submission form view. The Submission model contains instructor_notes marked as 'Internal-only notes never shown to students.' Students can access this view when editing their submissions.

WebhookForm.clean_target_url() uses an incomplete denylist that only blocks 'localhost', '127.0.0.1', '::1', '0.0.0.0', and hostnames ending with '.internal' or '.local'. This misses RFC 1918 private IP ranges (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x), other loopback addresses (127.0.0.2, etc.), and DNS rebinding attacks.

AdminUserForm allows direct mass assignment of sensitive fields including 'role', 'is_active', and 'is_disabled' via the Meta fields configuration. While the view requires school_admin permissions, the form permits modification of all these fields in a single operation without additional confirmation.

The login_view function logs user-controlled email addresses from failed login attempts via log_action() metadata without sanitization. Attackers can inject newlines or special characters to forge log entries or corrupt audit trails.

The admin_user_edit view logs the 'changes' dictionary containing before/after values for role, is_disabled, and is_active fields. These values come directly from user form input and are passed to log_action() without sanitization.
The admin_invitation_create view logs user-controlled email and role values from the invitation form via log_action() metadata without sanitization.
The manage_api_keys view logs API key labels (from user form input) via log_action() metadata without sanitization.
The manage_webhooks view logs the webhook event type (from user form input) via log_action() metadata without sanitization.
The submission_form view logs original filenames from user-uploaded files via log_action() metadata without sanitization. Attackers can control filenames in uploaded files.
The submission_attachment_download view logs the original_filename from the attachment object (which came from user-uploaded file) via log_action() without sanitization.

The grading_queue view loads all submissions for an assignment using Submission.objects.filter(assignment=a).select_related('student') without any pagination or limit. For assignments with thousands of submissions, this loads all records into memory.

The submission_attachment_download function attempts to prevent path traversal by checking if file_path starts with media_root_real + os.sep. However, this check may be bypassable on certain operating systems or with specific Unicode normalization attacks. The path sanitization logic is at line 12 in assignments/models.py which only replaces '..' and '/', but this may not cover all path traversal vectors.
The default database connection string 'postgres://lms:lms@localhost:5432/lms' does not specify SSL/TLS parameters (sslmode=require). This can result in unencrypted transmission of database traffic.
The raw request body is decoded and logged without sanitization. Attackers can inject control characters, newlines, or fake log entries into the application logs.
The endpoint uses MD5 hash algorithm which is cryptographically broken and should not be used for any security-sensitive operations.
The endpoint explicitly disables XSS protection and clears Content-Security-Policy, weakening the browser's security defenses.
The original_filename from uploaded files is passed to log_action metadata without sanitization. Attackers can inject newlines or special characters into filenames to tamper with audit logs.

SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE are set to 'not DEBUG', meaning the Secure flag is not set on cookies when DEBUG=True. If debug mode is accidentally enabled in production, session cookies will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections.
DEBUG mode is read from an environment variable without additional safeguards. Debug mode exposes sensitive information like stack traces, settings, and internal paths.

The template displays user email addresses ({{ t.author.email }}) in the discussion board list view. Email addresses are personally identifiable information (PII) and should not be exposed to other users in a discussion forum. This exposes users to increased risk of spam, phishing, and privacy violations. The typical pattern is to display display_name or username instead.

The template exposes the thread author's email address ({{ thread.author.email }}) in the thread detail view. Email addresses are PII and should not be displayed to other users without explicit consent. This appears in the metadata line showing author information.
The template exposes comment author email addresses ({{ c.author.email }}) for each comment in a thread. This exposes PII for every participant in the discussion to every other participant.

The template includes a hidden form field with name="next" containing {{ n.url }} which is used for post-action redirect. If the notification URL field can be manipulated to contain an external URL (e.g., https://attacker.com), submitting this form would redirect the user to an attacker-controlled site. This is commonly used in phishing attacks.

The discussion board template exposes user email addresses (PII) to all course participants. Line 18 renders `{{ t.author.email|default:"—" }}` which displays the author's email address. In a discussion forum context, this exposes personally identifiable information to other students. The system has a display_name field (as evidenced in student_dashboard.html) that should be used for identification instead of email addresses.

The thread detail template exposes the thread author's email address to all viewers. Line 13 renders `{{ thread.author.email|default:"—" }}` which displays the author's email. This exposes PII in a discussion context where participants should be identified by display name rather than email address.

The thread detail template exposes comment author email addresses. Line 19 renders `{{ c.author.email|default:"—" }}` for each comment, displaying the comment author's email to all viewers. This exposes PII and should use display_name instead.

A hidden form input renders the notification URL directly without escaping: value="{{ n.url }}". If the URL field contains attacker-controlled data with quote characters or JavaScript payloads, it can break out of the attribute context and execute arbitrary code when the form is rendered.

The SignupByInviteForm only checks if the password is literally 'password' (case-insensitive) and enforces a minimum length of 10 characters. It does not use Django's built-in password validators (e.g., CommonPasswordValidator, NumericPasswordValidator), allowing weak passwords.
Transport errors during webhook delivery are captured with full exception details in the response_body field, which is stored in the database and potentially visible to admin users.

The api_me endpoint uses @csrf_exempt decorator. While this endpoint uses Bearer token authentication (not cookie-based sessions), the CSRF exemption is applied. Since the endpoint uses API key authentication rather than session cookies, CSRF is not exploitable here.
The api_courses endpoint uses @csrf_exempt decorator. Since it uses Bearer token authentication and @require_safe (GET only), CSRF is not exploitable.
The api_assignments endpoint uses @csrf_exempt decorator. Since it uses Bearer token authentication and @require_safe (GET only), CSRF is not exploitable.
The api_my_grades endpoint uses @csrf_exempt decorator. Since it uses Bearer token authentication and @require_safe (GET only), CSRF is not exploitable.
The course_vault_stash_234 function uses a hardcoded default SSN value '111-22-3333' when writing data to a file. While this appears to be test data, it represents hardcoded PII in the source code.

User-provided search parameters (q, action, actor_email) are passed to the template context and displayed. While Django templates auto-escape HTML, if logs are exported to text formats, injection could occur.
